title: A lamp for the path
hookLine: Atisha's short text sets out the stages of the path
carry: has the aim grown its wings

lines: A SMALL LAMP, A DARK TRAIL.
cards: A hiker at the edge of a dark trail doesn't need the whole mountain lit up. A small lamp will do, if it shows the next few steps and roughly where they lead.
Atisha, the Indian teacher whose coming to Tibet brought a renewal, was asked by a Tibetan ruler, tradition says, for something simple: not a library, but a guide a person could carry.
What Atisha wrote is short, and its title says what it's for.

teach.b: It's the Lamp for the Path to Awakening. We met its outline when Atisha first came to Tibet; today, a closer look inside. The opening verses sort readers not by school but by aim.
Some seek good things for themselves within the round of lives. Some turn from that round toward their own peace. And some want to end the suffering of others as if it were their own.
The Lamp says plainly that the rest is written for that third person.
It asks them to take refuge and raise the wish to awaken for everyone's sake, the same wish we heard from Shantideva, and then to keep vows. A wish with no conduct behind it stays a wish.

teach.h: A BIRD WITHOUT WINGS CAN'T FLY.
teach.b: For meditation, Atisha uses a plain picture: a bird whose wings haven't grown can't fly. Without a settled, steady mind, he says, a person can't do much good for others. So calm comes first.

Near the end, the Lamp says that wisdom without skillful means is bondage, and skillful means without wisdom is bondage too, so keep both. Insight with no kindness binds; kindness with no insight binds another way.
Later Tibetan teachers wrote whole books on this outline, a genre called lamrim, the stages of the path. The Lamp itself is short enough to carry, which was the point.

how: Atisha's Lamp for the Path to Awakening is studied in Tibetan monasteries and retreat centers, and its outline of three kinds of practitioner shapes the lamrim, the stages-of-the-path teachings given in Tibetan Buddhist communities.

o: the stages of the path, laid out step by step
a Tibetan word for a mountain pilgrim trail
a lamp lit before Tibetan shrines each night

games.q: a lamp for the path: tap the pairs.

s: the Lamp says wisdom alone is enough
it calls wisdom without skillful means bondage, and means without wisdom too.
the Lamp is written for the person with the great aim
the one who wants to end others' suffering as if it were their own.
the Lamp sorts people by which school they belong to
it sorts them by what they're aiming at.

games.q: you're Atisha, asked by a Tibetan ruler for help. the teaching in the land is tangled. what do you give him?
o: a vast library of every text from India.
a short guide that lays out the stages by aim.
a list of who is right and who is wrong.
games.why: Atisha wrote a short text, the Lamp, sorting the path into stages by what a person is aiming at.

practice: Ask quietly, with a breath between each question: what do I want for my own life this year, what would real peace look like underneath that, and what would I wish for the people around me, all of them?
Let one answer come for each, in your own words, then rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Lamrim. The stages of the path, the genre Atisha's short text for Tibetan practice gave rise to, sorting the path by aim. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit for awakening, the first word of the text's Sanskrit title, Bodhipathapradipa: lamp for the path to awakening.

carryVoice: Your line: has the aim grown its wings. A small lamp, a few steps, and the great aim still ahead. Go gently.

sources.ref: Atisha, Bodhipathapradipa (Lamp for the Path to Awakening)
